title: Overridden Safeties (The Silent Warning Compiler)
pattern: Systematically silencing compiler warnings, turning off static analyzer rules, or commenting out failing test suites in order to expedite development or "clean up" the build output.
why_bad: It overrides safety rails. Critical warnings (such as ignoring a `Result` that could indicate database failure) are silenced, making the build pass superficially while leaving the runtime unstable and prone to silent data corruption (Chernobyl pattern).
detection: Directives that disable compiler warnings globally (e.g., `#![allow(warnings)]` or `#![allow(unused_must_use)]`) or commented-out assert statements in test files.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. Disabling highly specific, non-critical lint rules on legacy code is acceptable, but system-wide silence of safety diagnostics is defective.
fix: Resolve compiler warnings and failing tests directly rather than hiding them. Use explicit error-handling keywords (like `?` or `match`) on variables returned from volatile functions.
source: Robert C. Martin, *Clean Code*, Chapter 17, G4 ("Overridden Safeties").
